```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = NA)
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")

bayesplot::bayesplot_theme_set(ggplot2::theme_gray())
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "brightblue")
```

This tutorial introduces to data augmentation with the package `housepi`.
We explain the process of associating augmented variable to individuals to then proceed with standard model generation and inference.

# Estimate Incubation Periods Distribution

For simplicity, we start testing data augmentation on a dataset which is not a household survey.
Instead we consider a simulated report documenting the days when a number of cases were exposed to infection and the days of symptom onset.

Assuming the incubation period to be described by a gamma distribution, we want to estimate the respective parameters augmenting the exposure and onset times, modeled as uniformly distributed in the reported ranges.
We associate a positive status to all individuals and we correct for right censoring modifying the maximum values as follows:

```{r}
dataset <- housepi::delays
dataset$exposure_max <- dataset$exposure_max + 0.999
dataset$onset_max <- dataset$onset_max + 0.999
dataset$status <- 1

head(dataset)
```

We generate the model as showed in the [Walkthrough](walkthrough.html):

```{r}
# generate an instance of the household model class
hhmodel <- housepi::HouseholdModel$new("augm-incubation-from-delays")

# gamma distribution parameter definitions
hhmodel$load_param_list(
  shape = list(prior = "unif", args = c(max = 5), rule = "norm"),
  scale = list(prior = "unif", args = c(max = 5), rule = "norm")
)
```

## Build Augmented Variables

Similarly to parameter, augmented variables require definitions for models and proposer rules needed for the Bayesian Monte Carlo.
In many applications, augmented variable definitions can also depend on the dataset or on model parameters to be inferred.

We can link an argument value to its origin with the character "\@", e.
g.
"column\@D" will link to the value at individual row and "column".
More in general, definition arguments `value`, `args`, `min`, `max`, `scale` and `from` can be linked to external values in the following ways

| Origin    | Link Examples       |
|-----------|---------------------|
| Scalar    | 17, "17", "17\@S"   |
| Parameter | "alpha", "alpha\@P" |
| Dataset   | "onset_date\@D"     |

Here we associate to each individual an exposure and an onset time.

```{r}
# add 'exposure' time definition
hhmodel$add_augm(
  name = "exposure",
  value = "exposure_min@D", # start from data value 'exposure_min'
  model = "unif",
  args = c(min = "exposure_min@D",  # move within the range 'exposure_min'
           max = "exposure_max@D"), # and 'exposure_max'
  rule = "norm", # normal distribution for the mcmc proposer 
  scale = 0.25   # with scale 0.25 (i. e. standard deviation)
)

# add 'onset' time definition
hhmodel$add_augm(
  name = "onset",
  value = "onset_max@D",
  model = "unif",
  args = c(min = "onset_min@D",
           max = "onset_max@D"),
  rule = "norm", 
  scale = 0.25
)
```

We can inspect our current augmented variable definitions by calling the field `$augm_defs`:

```{r}
augm_defs <- hhmodel$augm_defs
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(augm_defs[1:9],
             caption = "Augmented variable definitions 1/2.")
knitr::kable(augm_defs[10:(dim(augm_defs)[2])],
             caption = "Augmented variable definitions 2/2.")
  
```

### Extract Augmented Variable Traces

We could run the inference and extract the results as usual.
However, sometimes we might be interested in extracting also to check if augmented variables evolve as expected.
We can do so by providing the `id` of individual augmented variables we want to store, in the setup arguments of `$infer()` method:

```{r}
# ask for the traces of augmented variables for individual with id 7
hhmodel$infer(dataset = dataset, n_steps = 10000, n_burnin = 500, thin = 8,
              n_chains = 4, n_adapt = 2000, seed = 4349, progress = FALSE, 
              id_trace = 7) 
```

Note: The warning tells us that our dataset has no demographic structure: it will be interpreted as single individuals living in separate households.

```{r, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4, fig.fullwidth=TRUE, out.height="auto", fig.align="center"}
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(hhmodel$traces)
```

## Other Proposer Rules for the Augmented Variables

```{r, include=FALSE}
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "purple")
```

When it comes to data augmentation, we might need to explore different options for the Monte Carlo moves.
In the following examples we show the differences between move choices that can be performed.
As shown in the vignette [Bayesian MCMC options](bayesian_mcmc_options.html), we do the testing with the "blank" model.
We always recommend a visual assesment before choosing a new move.

```{r}
# use default "blank" model to show some tests
hhmodel <- housepi::HouseholdModel$new("blank")
```

```{r, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=2, fig.fullwidth=TRUE, out.height="auto", fig.align="center"}
# with model (default Gibbs rule)
hhmodel$drop_all()
hhmodel$add_augm(name = "move_with_model", model = "norm")
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(hhmodel$infer(progress = FALSE, seed = 1)$traces)

# random walk starting from 0 (without model)
hhmodel$drop_all()
hhmodel$add_augm(name = "random_walk", value = 0, rule = "norm")
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(hhmodel$infer(progress = FALSE, seed = 2)$traces)

# independent normal moves from value 87 (without model)
hhmodel$drop_all()
hhmodel$add_augm(name = "independent_moves", rule = "norm", from = 87)
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(hhmodel$infer(progress = FALSE, seed = 3)$traces)
```

### A Note on Inverse Temperatures

```{r, include=FALSE}
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "orange")
```

```{r}
# with model (default Gibbs rule)
hhmodel$drop_all()
hhmodel$add_augm(name = "tempered", model = "norm", rule = "norm")
```

```{r, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=2, fig.fullwidth=TRUE, out.height="auto", fig.align="center"}
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(hhmodel$infer(progress = FALSE, seed = 1, inv_temper = 0.01)$traces)
```
